name: Benzophenone-9
lead: Benzophenone-9 (BP-9) is a water-soluble benzophenone-type ultraviolet-absorbing compound that appears in lists of sunscreen and UV-filter ingredients. Published material on it is sparse and consists mostly of environmental and analytical chemistry rather than studies of cosmetic benefit.[1][2]

In a 2022 study of 196 paired urine and blood samples from young adults in South China, benzophenone-7 and benzophenone-9 were not detected in any sample, while other benzophenone-type filters were widely found.[1] A 2017 laboratory study examined how BP-9 and benzophenone-4 break down under a UV/hydrogen peroxide water-treatment process, identifying 17 degradation products for BP-9.[2]

paras: BP-9 is listed among benzophenone UV filters used to absorb ultraviolet light in sunscreen-type products. A laboratory study of water sterilisation by pulsed spark discharge reported that adding 30 mg/L of BP-9 completely suppressed the UV-driven inactivation of bacteria, illustrating its UV-absorbing behaviour.[3] Researchers have also studied organic UV absorbers of this kind as components of layered double hydroxide materials.[4]

Benzophenone-type UV filters as a group are described in the research literature as endocrine-disrupting chemicals found in consumer and personal-care products.[1] In the South China study, BP-9 was among the compounds not detected in either urine or blood.[1] Transformation studies of BP-9 in water have focused on environmental fate rather than effects on skin.[2]

No studies found. The related literature consists of laboratory, analytical and environmental work on benzophenone UV filters rather than human trials of BP-9 for skin protection or appearance.[1][2][3]

card.summary: A water-soluble benzophenone UV filter with almost no published human data; mostly appears in environmental chemistry papers.
card.note: Very little published research on cosmetic use.

quick.overview:
Benzophenone-9 is a water-soluble ultraviolet-absorbing chemical listed among benzophenone sunscreen filters.

Published work on it is thin: a few environmental and laboratory studies, and no human trials of its skin-protective effect.
quick.mechanism: Like other benzophenones, it absorbs ultraviolet light. A lab study found it blocked UV-driven bacterial killing in water.
quick.risks: A 2022 study did not detect it in urine or blood samples from young adults. Benzophenone filters as a group have been described as endocrine-disrupting chemicals in the literature; BP-9 itself has little safety data in the sources reviewed.
